## Proof

Let $g = |f|$. Then $g \colon \Omega \to [0,\infty)$ is a non-negative measurable function. For each $\alpha \ge 0$, define the level set
$$A_\alpha = \{\omega \in \Omega : g(\omega) = \alpha\}.$$

**Key observation.** The family $\{A_\alpha\}_{\alpha \ge 0}$ is pairwise disjoint, and $\bigcup_{\alpha \ge 0} A_\alpha = \Omega$. Indeed, every $\omega$ has a single value $g(\omega)$, so $\omega$ belongs to exactly one level set $A_{g(\omega)}$.

**Counting the level sets of positive measure.** Since $\mu$ is a probability measure, $\mu(\Omega)=1$. For any integer $n \ge 1$, consider the collection
$$S_n = \{\alpha \ge 0 : \mu(A_\alpha) \ge 1/n\}.$$

If $\alpha_1, \dots, \alpha_k$ are distinct elements of $S_n$, then by disjointness,
$$\sum_{i=1}^{k} \mu(A_{\alpha_i}) = \mu\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{k} A_{\alpha_i}\right) \le \mu(\Omega) = 1.$$
Since each term is $\ge 1/n$, we get $k/n \le 1$, i.e. $k \le n$. Thus $S_n$ is **finite** (has at most $n$ elements).

Now the set of "bad" values where the level set has positive measure is
$$\{\alpha \ge 0 : \mu(A_\alpha) > 0\} = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} S_n,$$
since $\mu(A_\alpha) > 0$ iff $\mu(A_\alpha) \ge 1/n$ for some $n$. This is a countable union of finite sets, hence **countable**.

**Conclusion.** The set
$$\{\alpha \ge 0 : \mu\{\omega : |f(\omega)| = \alpha\} > 0\}$$
is at most countable. Equivalently, $\mu\{\omega : |f(\omega)| = \alpha\} = 0$ for all but countably many $\alpha$.

**Remark.** The argument uses only that $\mu$ is a finite measure and that $g = |f|$ is measurable; the integrability of $f$ is not needed. The essential point is that a finite measure can charge at most countably many disjoint atoms of a measurable partition, and the level sets of a measurable function form such a partition.
